A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DT-VIN research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, experiments, tables and figures can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original maze and ViZDoom experiments, component ablations, depth comparisons and computational measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds continuous-control, terrain-image navigation, robustness, ablation and scaling results.

M1.justification: The core dynamic transition, softmax and adaptive highway mechanism remain. v2 adds task-specific adaptations, including continuous-control pretraining and a state-conditioned action head, plus shared CNN encoders for rover imagery (Appendices D–E). The written loss also changes from 1/K to 1/(K|D|) with the same K definition; whether this reflects an implementation change is unexplained.

E1.justification: v2 extends the maze/ViZDoom evaluation to Point Maze and Ant Maze continuous control and Apollo 17 terrain-image navigation. It also adds differential-drive, eight-neighbor movement and controlled noisy-observation scenarios. Although detailed 25×25 comparison plots disappear, that maze size remains represented in scaling experiments.

E2.justification: VIN, GPPN and Highway VIN remain the principal comparators. v2 adds an evaluated CNN+A* baseline for rover navigation (Table 3), combining learned obstacle classification with classical search. Newly discussed methods such as MuZero and implicit differentiable planners are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include continuous-control training on 9×12 layouts followed by evaluation on unseen 35×35 and 100×100 mazes, terrain preprocessing and elevation-based labels, and data/depth sweeps. GPPN is now reported at 5000 layers, previously excluded. Section 4 also revises SPL and optimality definitions toward expert-path lengths and relative optimality; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 separates state-dependent and observation-dependent kernel ablations, adds obstacle-count and loss analyses, learned-kernel visualizations, gradient measurements and additional highway variants (Figures 6–7). Appendices C, F and G add noise and movement robustness, approximate-path-length tests, highway-spacing sensitivity, reduced-data experiments and computational/sample/depth scaling analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting. However, v2 Figure 3 omits the DT-VIN uncertainty bands visible in v1's 100×100 success-rate and optimality-rate panels. The corresponding success-rate table retains standard deviations. No change in run count or statistical testing is reported.

E6.justification: Many results are added, including 93.26±3.14% success for DT-VIN versus 61.78±6.12% for GPPN on 100×100 Ant Maze (v2 Table 2). The original maze success table is preserved as Table 7, while detailed 25×25 comparison curves are removed. For the stated 600-layer, 35×35, 30-epoch configuration, DT-VIN memory changes from 53.3 to 7.2 GB and training time from 12.1 to 12.3 hours, without explaining the revision.

T1.justification: Section 4 replaces globally minimum-length optimality with minimum length among expert and compared-model solutions, a substantive definition change. Appendix B.2 newly argues that CNN-generated dynamic kernels preserve translation equivariance. These are limited mathematical additions rather than a new theorem or substantial proof development.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden demonstrated applicability and performance claims from 2D/ViZDoom navigation to continuous control and rover navigation. The central 5000-layer contribution remains. The conclusion also drops v1's claim of 'exponentially' longer-term and larger-scale planning, retaining the narrower scaling claim.

C2.justification: v1 explicitly lists knowing the shortest-path length as a limitation; v2 instead discusses usable non-expert and heuristic estimates with measured penalties (Appendix F.2). v2 adds explanations involving compounded transition errors, disruption from intermediate skip connections, and interpretations of model/data scaling and computational costs (Section 4.4 and Appendix G).

D1.justification: v2 supplies continuous-control and rover architectures, hyperparameters, dataset identities, pretraining instructions and terrain-label construction. It newly documents maze-layout separation between training and testing, the maze policy head and ViZDoom spatial units. GPU-hour accounting supplements wall-clock measurements. These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained maze splits.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning relative to classical search, explicit learned world models and Zhao et al.'s implicit differentiable planners, plus diffusion planners as a future integration direction. Imitation-learning and new dataset references are added, while CNN-background references are removed. The central relationship to VIN, GPPN and Highway VIN remains.

P1.justification: The introduction and preliminaries are rewritten to emphasize imitation learning and distinguish planning scale from horizon. The method explanation separates two kinds of kernel dependence. Ablations become a separate subsection, ViZDoom and limitations move into appendices, and supplementary material is extensively reorganized into method, task, ablation and scaling sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 3 is rearranged and loses its 25×25 panels; ablations expand into Figures 6–7 with new diagnostics. Numerous task illustrations and tables are added. The original success table and ViZDoom figure move to appendix Table 7 and Figure 11.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow evaluation and limited component diagnosis through continuous-control and terrain tasks, separated kernel ablations, gradient measurements, and tests of approximate path lengths and scaling. These additions provide stronger evidence about generality, mechanisms and applicability limits. Unexplained loss/resource revisions and omitted uncertainty bands remain reporting weaknesses, but the broader diagnostic evidence and implementation documentation provide a substantial net improvement.
